name: Progresa/Oportunidades (Mexico)
summary: Mexican conditional cash transfer program created in 1997 (later called Oportunidades and Prospera). It paid poor families, mostly mothers, on the condition that children attend school and the family attend health checkups. It was evaluated from the start with a randomized experiment and served as a model for dozens of countries, including for Bolsa Família.
mechanism: Cash relieves immediate poverty; conditions encourage investment in children's education and health, with the aim of reducing poverty in the next generation.

findings.result: In a systematic review of cash transfer programs, both conditional and unconditional transfers raise enrollment and attendance; programs with explicit, monitored and enforced conditions have substantively larger effects (60% improvement in the odds of enrollment).
In the same review, the effect of cash transfers on test scores is small at best.
In a Gini decomposition, conditional transfers accounted for about 21% of the fall in inequality in Mexico between the mid-1990s and the mid-2000s, despite being less than 1% of total income.

external_validity: Progresa started in poor rural communities and was evaluated there. Bolsa Família is national and has design and implementation features that set it apart from a conditional cash transfer strictly focused on human capital (Soares, Ribas and Osório, 2010). Since the systematic review finds larger effects when conditions are explicit, monitored and enforced, Progresa's results do not transfer automatically to Brazil.
limitations: The systematic review pools studies of several programs and countries; the enrollment effect is not an estimate for Progresa alone.
The share of the fall in inequality attributed to transfers comes from an accounting decomposition, not a causal estimate.
Many program outcomes were tested at once. The review by Parker and Todd (2017) re-examines effects correcting for multiple hypothesis testing; check it before citing a single effect.
